newsitem.title: USA: House votes to ban U.S. funds for suicide help.
newsitem.headline: House votes to ban U.S. funds for suicide help.

text.p: The House of Representatives voted overwhelmingly on Thursday to ban federal funds for physician-assisted suicide, entering an emotional battle unfolding across the country about how suffering people die.

The measure is largely symbolic at this point because no state allows assisted suicide and no federal program pays for it. But the Supreme Court is considering two cases that could establish a constitutional right to assisted suicide or pave the way for states to legalize it. A ruling is expected in July.
The bill passed 398 to 16, with the dissenting votes coming from Democrats. The Senate has not taken up a companion bill, but House sponsors expected that to happen shortly.
President Bill Clinton has made clear his opposition to physician-assisted suicide and his spokesman Mike McCurry said the president would sign this bill.
The bill would not prevent terminally ill people from refusing medical treatment, food or hydration as they neared the end of life, options that have become widely acceptable in U.S. society.

It also would not bar patients from getting pain medication, even though some of those drugs can slow breathing and may hasten death. Doctors and ethicists recognize the distinction between drugs meant to control pain and large doses of drugs meant to end life.
Federal dollars "ought to be used to bring comfort and hope, not death," Virginia Republican Thomas Bliley, a leading backer of the bill, said.

Advocates of assisted suicide say mentally competent, terminally ill patients should have the right to decide when they are ready to die and to get the help they need to carry out that decision in a humane, dignified manner.

"It's sad when Congress makes medical decisions," said Faye Girsh, executive director of the Hemlock Society, a group that advocates self-determination for the sick. "If physician aid in dying is made legal, which I fully expect, only the rich will be able to afford death with dignity."

Critics, including the American Medical Association and other leading health groups, say doctors should help ease their patients' emotional and physical pain, not help kill them. Some also say there is a danger that legal suicide could lead to abuse and that patients could be coerced.

Anti-abortion groups have also joined the drive against assisted suicide, and the National Right to Life Committee called the House bill "a crucial pre-emptive strike to prevent tax dollars of American citizens from being used to fund legalized killing."

One of the few dissenting voices, Jim McDermott, a Washington Democrat who is one of the most liberal members of Congress, said the law was simplistic and vague and failed to define adequately what constitutes physician-assisted suicide.
"No one on this floor is for physician-assisted suicide -- not even me," said McDermott, a psychiatrist who entered politics. "But I'm going to vote against this bill."

Ralph Hall, a conservative Texas Democrat who drafted the bill, told fellow lawmakers that if they failed to pass it and the Supreme Court allowed assisted suicide, "You would open up the Treasury to Dr. Kevorkians around the country." He was referring to Jack Kevorkian, the Michigan pathologist who has assisted numerous suicides in defiance of state laws.
The bill was handled under a special procedure so no amendments were allowed and passage required a two-thirds vote.

Earlier, in committee hearings, Democrats had tried and failed to add amendments that would require medical schools to improve training on end-of-life issues. Republicans fought that as government meddling in medical schools, but agreed to set up some pilot projects aimed at improving palliative care.
